book: DK China, DK Travel, 2026 (ISBN електронної версії 9798217309900)

pois.name: Palace Wall
pois.text: The wall around the Forbidden City is marked at each corner by an elaborate Arrow Tower, notable for their many eaves. The northern gate of the palace is called Shenwu Men or the Gate of Divine Prowess, and served as a combined bell and drum tower.

pois.name: Inner Court
pois.text: A short distance beyond the Hall of Preserving Harmony (Outer Court) lies a long but narrow courtyard. The gates here lead to the open areas east and west of the Outer Court and a main gate, the Gate of Heavenly Purity, opening to the Inner Court. Here lie three splendid palaces. The double-eaved Palace of Heavenly Purity was used as the imperial sleeping quarters and for the reception of officials. The highlight inside the palace is the beautiful imperial throne surrounded by candles and mirrors to ward off evil spirits.

pois.name: Imperial Garden
pois.text: The Imperial Garden, just north of the three inner palaces and the Gate of Earthly Tranquility, dates from the reign of the Ming Yongle emperor. It is symmetrically laid out with pavilions, temples, and halls as well as a rock garden and ancient trees. The pavilions at each of the four corners symbolize the seasons. The most famous of these are the charming Thousand Autumns Pavilion and Ten Thousand Springs Pavilion, each topped with a circular roof. On top of a lofty rockery in the northeast of the garden, the Imperial View Pavilion enjoys views over the gardens and beyond.

pois.name: Eastern Palaces
pois.text: On the east side of the Inner Court lies a much closer-knit series of smaller palaces and courtyards formerly used as the residences of imperial concubines. Some of these serve as museums of jade, paintings, enamels, and other antique collectibles, including the impressive Clock and Watch Exhibition Hall (in the Palace of Eternal Harmony). To the southeast of the Inner Court is the Palace of Abstinence, and, farther southeast, stands a beautiful Nine Dragon Screen, a 100-ft- (30-m-) long spirit wall, or screen, made from richly glazed tiles. Jewelry displays are housed in a series of halls in

pois.name: Western Palaces
pois.text: Parts of the western flank of the Forbidden City are closed to visitors, but the halls west of the three inner palaces are accessible. The Hall of Mental Cultivation was used by the Yongzheng emperor as his residence. The East Warm Chamber of the Hall of Mental Cultivation was the site of the abdication of Pu Yi (see Changchun ) , the last emperor, in 1912.

pois.name: National Museum of China
pois.text: Spread over more than 2 million sq ft (191,900 sq m), the National Museum of China is thought to be the largest museum in the world. It houses an exceptional collection of ancient treasures and cultural relics, including ceramics, bronzes, jade artifacts, and calligraphy. Two permanent exhibitions cover China’s ancient history and notable events from 1840 to the present day; however, the chaos of the Cultural Revolution is glossed over with barely a mention.

pois.name: Dazhalan and Liulichang
pois.text: Southeast of Tiananmen Square are the narrow and lively hutongs (see Beijing’s Courtyard Houses ) of the old Chinese quarter, with Dazhalan and Liulichang being the most popular. The entire quarter has been renovated to re-create the Qing dynasty era, complete with a tourist tram and a host of shops and restaurants.

pois.name: Xuanwumen Catholic Church
pois.text: Also known as the South Cathedral, Xuanwumen was the first Catholic church to be built in Beijing. It stands on the site of Jesuit Matteo Ricci’s former residence. Ricci was the first Jesuit missionary to reach Beijing and gained the favor of the Wanli emperor to establish this church.

pois.name: Legation Quarter
pois.text: After the Second Opium War, foreign delegations took up residence in a quarter located southeast of the Forbidden City. Known as the Legation Quarter, this is where the first modern foreign buildings in Beijing took root.

pois.name: Qian Men
pois.text: Qian Men (Front Gate) consists of two towers, the Zhengyang Men (Facing the Sun Gate), on the southern edge of Tiananmen Square, and the Jian Lou (Arrow Tower). Zhengyang Men was the most imposing of the nine gates in Beijing’s inner city wall.

pois.name: Jing Shan Park
pois.text: Situated on Beijing’s north-south axis, Jing Shan Park has its origins in the Yuan dynasty (1279-1368). Its hill was created from earth that was excavated while building the moat around the Forbidden City. In the early years of the Ming dynasty, it was known as Wansui Shan (Long Life Hill), but was renamed Jing Shan (View or Prospect Hill) in the Qing era. Foreign residents also referred to it as Mei Shan (Coal Hill), supposedly because coal was stored at the foot of the hill.

pois.name: Bei Hai Park
pois.text: An imperial garden for more than 1,000 years, this park, also known as the Winter Palace, was opened to the public in 1925. Filled with artificial hills, pavilions, and temples, it is associated with Kublai Khan, who redesigned it during the Mongol Yuan dynasty. The Tuancheng (Round City) near the south entrance has a decorated jade urn that once belonged to him. The park is named after its lake, Bei Hai, the southern end of which is bordered by the inaccessible Zhong Nan Hai, the headquarters of the Communist Party. In the middle of the lake is Jade Island, topped by the 118-ft- (36-m-) high

pois.name: Prince Gong’s Mansion
pois.text: Situated in a charming hutong district west of Qian Hai, Prince Gong’s mansion is Beijing’s most complete example of a historic mansion. It was supposedly the inspiration behind the residence portrayed by Cao Xueqin in his classic 18th-century novel Dream of the Red Chamber .

pois.name: Drum and Bell Towers
pois.address: Northern end of Di’anmen Wai Dajie, Dongcheng
pois.text: Located on the north-south meridian that bisects the Forbidden City and Tiananmen Square, the Drum Tower (Gu Lou) rises up from a historic Beijing hutong district. The structure was first built in 1420 during the reign of the Ming Yongle emperor.

pois.name: Di Tan Park
pois.address: N of the Lama Temple, Dongcheng
pois.text: A peaceful and lush space, Di Tan is home to the Temple of Earth, which gives the park its name and was once the venue for imperial ceremonies. The park’s altar, Fangze Tan, dates back to the Ming dynasty. Under the Ming, five main altars were established at the city’s cardinal points - the Temple of Heaven in the south, Di Tan in the north, Ri Tan (Temple of the Sun) in the east, Yue Tan (Temple of the Moon) in the west, and Sheji Tan (Temple of Land and Grain) in the center of the city.

pois.name: Lama Temple
pois.text: One of Beijing’s most beautiful temple complexes, the Lama Temple is also known as Yonghegong or the Palace of Peace and Harmony. Constructed in the late 17th century as a residence for Prince Yong, who went on to become Emperor Yongzheng, the temple was later occupied by Emperor Qianlong. In 1744, it was converted into a Tibetan lamasery.

pois.name: Confucius Temple
pois.text: Adjacent to the Lama Temple, the Confucius Temple is the largest in China outside Qufu, the philosopher’s birthplace in Shandong province. The alley leading to the temple has a fine pailou (decorative archway), few of which survive in Beijing. First built in 1302 during the Mongol Yuan dynasty, the temple served as the imperial college during the Yuan, Ming, and Qing dynasties. It was expanded in 1906 during the reign of Emperor Guangxu.

pois.name: Wangfujing Street
pois.text: Busy Wangfujing Street (Wangfujing Dajie), Beijing’s original shopping street, is lined with department stores and giant malls such as Beijing APM and WF Central, all of which are home to an excellent and varied line-up of Chinese and international boutiques and fine-dining restaurants. As well as big international brands, the street has a lively mix of traditional shops selling silk, tea, shoes, clothes, and a range of other local items.

pois.name: Dong Yue Miao
pois.text: On Beijing’s eastern side near Chaoyang’s Workers’ Stadium, this temple takes its name from the Daoist Eastern Peak, Dong Yue, also known as Tai Shan. It is fronted by a fabulous glazed Ming-dynasty paifang (decorative arch) inscribed with the characters Zhisi Daizong , meaning “offer sacrifices to Mount Tai (Tai Shan) in good order.”

pois.name: National Art Museum of China
pois.text: Founded by Mao Zedong in the early 1960s, the National Art Museum of China (Zhongguo Meishuguan) has 20 halls spread over five levels. It hosts rotating exhibitions of Chinese and international art, as well as occasional photography displays. Check the website for more information on current and upcoming exhibitions. Note, you’ll need to show your passport to be granted entry.

pois.name: Ancient Observatory
pois.text: Dating from 1442, Beijing’s ancient observatory (Gu Guanxiangtai) is one of the oldest in the world. It stands on a platform alongside a flyover off Jianguo Men Nei Dajie. A Yuan dynasty (1271-1368) observatory was also located here, but the structure that survives today was built after the Ming emperors relocated their capital from Nanjing to Beijing.

pois.name: Beijing Ancient Architecture Museum
pois.text: This museum is set inside the Ming-dynasty Xiannong temple complex. Starting in 1420, on the vernal equinox, the emperor would conduct sacrifices here, and then, dressed as a farmer, would plow furrows in a nearby field. The complex now houses Beijing’s first museum of architecture, covering Chinese building design from ancient to modern times.

pois.name: Capital Museum
pois.text: This striking glass and concrete structure houses some 200,000 relics arranged over seven stories, ranging from ancient bronze, porcelain, and jade to calligraphy and paintings. There is also an impressive collection of ancient Buddhist statues on display. Admission is free but book ahead for guaranteed entry.

pois.name: Cow Street Mosque
pois.text: Beijing’s oldest and largest mosque dates back to the 10th century. It is located in the city’s Hui District, near numerous Muslim restaurants and shops. The Hui, a Chinese Muslim minority group mainly from Ningxia province, are now scattered throughout China and number around 200,000 in Beijing. The men are easily identified by their beards and characteristic white hats.

pois.name: Southeast Corner Watchtower
pois.address: Off Jianguo Men Nan Dajie, Chongwen
pois.text: A short distance south of the Ancient Observatory, an imposing chunk of the Beijing city walls survives in the form of the 15th-century Southeast Corner Watchtower (Dongbian Men). After climbing onto the Ming-dynasty battlements, visitors can walk along the short but nonetheless impressive stretch of attached wall to admire the towering bastion, pitted with archers’ windows, and look down on the city below. The walls of the tower are engraved with graffiti left by soldiers of the international army that marched into the city to liberate the Foreign Legations during the Boxer Rebellion.

pois.name: Natural History Museum of China
pois.text: Housed in an enormous 1950s building, this museum is the largest of its type in China, with about 5,000 specimens arranged into three main collections: paleontology, zoology, and botany. The most interesting collection is found in the Paleontology Hall, which displays a selection of the dinosaurs and other prehistoric animals that populated China between 500 million and 1 million years ago. Exhibits to look out for include the large-handed Lufengosaurus from the early Jurassic period, and a skeleton of the spine-nosed Qingdaosaurus (Tsintaosaurus spinorhinus) from the late Cretaceous period, w

pois.name: Beijing Planning Exhibition Hall
pois.text: Just east of the historic Qian Men area, this exhibition traces the history of Beijing’s urban development through photographs, old maps, and models. The highlight is a huge scale model of the contemporary city, highlighting the latest development plans.

pois.name: Fayuan Temple
pois.text: A short walk east from Cow Street Mosque, the Fayuan Temple dates to 696 CE and is probably the oldest temple in Beijing. It was consecrated by the Tang Taizong emperor (r. 626-49) to commemorate the soldiers who perished in an expedition against the northern tribes. The original Tang-era buildings were destroyed by a succession of natural disasters, and the temple has been rebuilt several times over its 1,300-year history. The present structures date from the Ming (1368-1644) and Qing (1644-1912) eras.

pois.name: White Cloud Temple
pois.text: Home to the China Daoist Association, the White Cloud Temple (Baiyun Guan) was founded in 739 CE and is Beijing’s largest Daoist shrine. Known as the Temple of Heavenly Eternity, it was one of the three ancestral halls of the Quanzhen School of Daoism, which focused on right action and the benefits of good karma. Built largely of wood, the temple burned to the ground in 1166, and since then has been repeatedly destroyed and rebuilt. The structures that survive date largely from the Ming and Qing dynasties. A triple-gated Ming pailou stands at the entrance. According to local legend, rubbing th

pois.name: Military Museum of the Chinese People’s Revolution
pois.zh: 中国人民革命军事博物馆
pois.text: Topped by a gilded emblem of the People’s Liberation Army, the vast Military Museum of the Chinese People’s Revolution is mainly devoted to showcasing the military might of the PLA and documenting the revolutionary wars led by the Chinese Communist Party in the 20th century. Visitors are greeted by paintings of Mao, Marx, Lenin, and Stalin. The first floor features gleaming fighter jets, tanks, and surface-to-air missiles, while the top gallery chronicles the military campaigns of the People’s Republic of China. The east wing of the second floor is dedicated to the military history of imperial

pois.name: White Tower Temple
pois.text: Instantly recognizable by its distinctive 167-ft (51-m) white Tibetan-style dagoba (stupa or funerary mound) designed by a Nepalese architect, the White Tower Temple (Miaoying Si) dates to 1271, when Beijing was under Mongol rule. In addition to its conventional Drum and Bell Towers, Hall of Heavenly Kings, and Main Halls, this Buddhist temple has a remarkable collection of small Tibetan Buddhist statues and a collection of 18 bronze luohan (disciples).

pois.name: National Center for the Performing Arts
pois.text: This futuristic performance space stages classical concerts, plays, and Chinese operas. When the building opened in 2007, it was nicknamed the “Giant Egg” due to its sleek dome. Inside are a state-of-the-art opera house and concert halls of varying sizes. Daytime guided tours offer a look at its grand interiors.

pois.name: Badaling
pois.text: Equipped with guardrails, cable car, pristine watchtowers, and tourist facilities, the restored Ming fortification at Badaling is the most popular section of the Great Wall, and the easiest to reach from Beijing. To fully appreciate the breathtaking view of the wall winding its way over the hills, get away from the crowds by walking as far as you can along the wall either east or west of the entrance.

pois.name: Mutianyu
pois.address: 46 miles (75 km) N of Beijing, Mutianyu town, Huairou County
pois.text: The appeal of Mutianyu lies in its dramatic hilly setting and slightly less intrusive tourist industry than at Badaling. The wall here dates from 1368 and follows the same route as an earlier fortification erected during the Northern Qi dynasty (550-77 CE). Records indicate that Mutianyu served as signal towers, forts, living quarters, and storerooms.

pois.name: Simatai
pois.address: 68 miles (110 km) NE of Beijing, Miyun County
pois.text: The wall at Simatai has undergone only essential renovations, offering a more genuine impression of the original wall. This stretch can be accessed through Gubei Water Town, a tourist development designed in the style of a southern Chinese village, with historical exhibitions, hotels, shops, and restaurants. If you’re visiting later in the evening, you can see the Great Wall beautifully illuminated by spotlights from here.

pois.name: Jiankou
pois.text: Offering some of the best Great Wall scenery in China, the Jiankou section wraps around the former commune village of Xizhazi high up in Beijing’s northern mountains. Unrestored and thus not officially open to tourists, it nonetheless attracts adventurous hikers and amateur photographers seeking that iconic sunrise photo. Many of the battlements here are in a crumbling state of disrepair and very steep as they trace the ridgeline of mountains up to 3,000 ft (1,000 m) high, so it’s advisable to go with a guide.

pois.name: Jinshanling
pois.text: Constructed during the Ming dynasty, the Jinshanling section of the Great Wall zigzags dramatically over mountain country through a run of 67 watchtowers and five passes. The start of the tourist section has been fully restored and features a cable car that takes visitors up to the battlements, while at its edges the wall is in a more wild, untamed state.

pois.name: Gubeikou
pois.text: Gubeikou was a strategically vital stretch of the Ming Great Wall, and is particularly popular with hikers today. It has been left in a state of wistful dilapidation, with rows of crumbling watchtowers ascending into Beijing’s barren northern hills.

pois.name: Huanghuacheng
pois.address: 37 miles (60 km) N of Beijing, Huairou County
pois.text: On the same stretch of wall as Mutianyu, Huanghuacheng is a less-developed but exhilarating section. This “Lakeside Great Wall” spans a reservoir, creating an unmatched spectacle of the Great Wall dipping out of sight into the lake, and then emerging from the depths on the other side. A pedal boat ride is the best way to explore these battlements.

pois.name: Zhuangdaokou
pois.text: This steep section can be hiked near Zhuangdaokou village in the Huairou district. The route climbs through pretty countryside scenery to Huanghuacheng. The best way to reach Zhuangdaokou and other less-visited sections of the Great Wall is by renting a private car and driver.

pois.name: 798 Art District
pois.text: A hip development in a 1950s factory complex, the 798 Art District features dozens of galleries, design studios, restaurants, cafés, and shops, all showcasing Beijing’s thriving contemporary culture and art scene. It buzzes on weekends with a young, arty crowd, and increasingly with groups of out-of-town visitors. Many of the galleries are internationally owned, staging thought-provoking exhibitions by global superstars at the cutting edge of art. The gallery spaces themselves are former Bauhaus workshops, designed in the 1950s by East German consultants. Most of the galleries are closed on Mo

pois.name: Yuanming Yuan
pois.text: The Yuanming Yuan (Garden of Perfect Brightness, sometimes called the Old Summer Palace), now sits isolated from the main Summer Palace, but was once a collection of princely gardens fused into the main mass by the Qianlong emperor in the mid-18th century. The emperor commissioned Jesuits at his court to design and construct a set of European-style buildings in one corner, which they likened to Versailles. Unfortunately, all the traditional Chinese halls were looted, then burned down by British and French troops during the Second Opium War in 1860. Later the European-style buildings were pulle

pois.name: Xiang Shan Park
pois.text: This wooded area, also known as Fragrant Hills Park, is at its scenic best in the fall, when the maples turn red. Its main draws are the fine views from Incense Burner Peak, accessible by a chairlift, and Biyun Temple, or Azure Cloud Temple, near the main gate. The temple is guarded by the menacing deities Heng and Ha in the Mountain Gate Hall. A series of halls leads to the Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall, named for the founder of the Republic of China, whose coffin was temporarily stored here in 1925. At the temple’s rear is the Diamond Throne Pagoda.

pois.name: Beijing Olympic Park
pois.text: Beijing Olympic Park was designed as the stunning centerpiece of China’s massive building program for the 2008 Olympics. It is part of the city’s “Olympic Green” development, which includes a landscaped park, an Olympic Village, and many other stadia including the National Indoor Stadium and Swimming Center.

pois.name: Great Bell Temple
pois.text: Home to a fantastic collection of bells, the 18th-century Dazhong Si (Great Bell Temple) follows a typical Buddhist layout. Its highlight is the 46.5-ton Yongle Bell in the rear tower. Cast between 1403 and 1424, it was brought here from Wanshou Temple during the reign of the Qianlong emperor. During the Ming and Qing dynasties, the bell was struck 108 times to bring in the New Year, and could be heard up to 25 miles (40 km) away. Visitors can pray for good luck by tossing a coin into the hole at the top of the bell.

pois.name: Tanzhe Temple
pois.metro: Pingguo Yuan (1 hr), then bus 931 or taxi
pois.address: Mentougou district, 28 miles (45 km) W of Beijing
pois.text: This enormous mountainside temple dates back to the 3rd century CE, when it was known as Jiafu Si. The temple is especially famous for its ancient trees, among which is a huge ginkgo known as the Emperor’s Tree.

pois.name: Marco Polo Bridge
pois.address: Wanping town, Fengtai, 10 miles (16 km) SW of city center
pois.text: Straddling the Yongding River in Wanping town, this 876-ft- (267-m-) long marble bridge was first built during the Jin dynasty in 1189 and has been restored and rebuilt several times since. Known as Lugou Qiao in Chinese, the bridge acquired its English name after the 13th-century explorer Marco Polo described it in his famous treatise The Travels . At the eastern and western ends are stelae inscribed by the Qing emperors Kangxi and Qianlong. A poetic observation by Qianlong on a stele at the eastern end reads “ lugou xiaoyue ,” meaning “moon at daybreak at Lugou.” The balustrades along the le

pois.name: Cuandixia
pois.metro: Pingguo Yuan (1 hr), then bus M11, M22 to Zhaitang (2 hrs) or taxi
pois.address: Near Zhaitang, 56 miles (90 km) NW of Beijing
pois.text: Despite the rather laborious expedition required to get here, a trip to Cuandixia is well worth the effort; the crumbling hamlet survives as a living museum of Ming- and Qing-dynasty village architecture. Situated on a steep mountainside, it is a pretty outpost of courtyard houses (siheyuan) and rural Chinese buildings. Because of the close-knit nature of the original village, all the courtyards were interconnected by small lanes. Look out for the Maoist graffiti that survives on the boundary walls; similar graffiti from the Cultural Revolution has been whitewashed in most other towns.

pois.name: Eastern Qing Tombs
pois.address: 77 miles (125 km) E of Beijing, Zunhua county, Hebei province
pois.text: The remoteness of the Eastern Qing Tombs makes them far less popular than the Ming ones, despite the fact that the setting is even more splendid . Of the many tombs scattered throughout the area, only five are the burial places of Qing emperors: Shunzhi (r. 1644-61), Kangxi (r. 1661-1722), Qianlong (r. 1735-95), and Xianfeng (r. 1851-61) are open, while that of Tongzhi (r. 1862-74) is not. A 3-mile (5-km) Spirit Way, an approach lined with guardian figures, leads to Shunzhi’s tomb, Xiao Ling, at the heart of the main tomb cluster. Southwest of here lies Yuling, Qianlong’s tomb, adorned with Bu

pois.name: Shamian Island
pois.address: North bank of Zhujiang River, Liwan district
pois.text: Leased to the French and British after the Chinese were defeated during the Second Opium War (1856-60), this island is really little more than a sandbank about half a mile (800 m) long. Before being allowed to settle on Shamian Island, foreigners had been compelled to remain in their warehouses on the mainland. Soon after the French settled at the east end and the British at the west, the streets filled with European-style villas, banks, and churches. Chinese people were long forbidden to set foot on the island, so an exclusively European way of life prevailed here. Its wide boulevards, open s

pois.name: Qingping Market
pois.text: Just across the water from Shamian Island is one of China’s largest and most famous markets, devoted to all types of produce. While primarily a herbal medicine market, it also sells spices, fruit, vegetables, dried seafood, grains, fish, and meat.

pois.name: Sacred Heart Church
pois.text: A Roman Catholic church, Sacred Heart (Sheng Xin DaJiaotang) was built by the French between 1863 and 1888. The church’s twin spires rise to a height of 190 ft (58 m), and its Bell Tower has four bronze bells cast in France.

pois.name: Peasant Movement Institute
pois.text: The city’s revolutionary past is on display in this former Ming Confucian temple. In 1924, the building became a training school for peasant revolutionaries, who were taught by leaders such as Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai . The endeavor was short-lived, however, and the school closed its doors in 1926 as the relationship between the Communists and the Kuomintang soured (see The Long March ) .

pois.name: Archaeological Site of the Palace of Nanyue Kingdom
pois.zh: 南越王博物院王宫展区
pois.text: This extraordinary site contains the excavated gardens that surrounded the palace of Zhao Tuo, the founder of the ancient Nanyue Kingdom . A Qin general from Hebei province, he founded an independent kingdom after the fall of the Qin dynasty, and ruled over much of what is now northern Vietnam and parts of south China. The site is covered by a corrugated roof, and a raised pathway leads past the main sights. To the northeast, a paved lake and a stream are clearly visible, while in the southwestern corner are the remains of an even older Qin-dynasty shipyard. The small on-site museum exhibits s

pois.name: Huaisheng Mosque
pois.text: Thought to have been founded during the Tang dynasty by Abu Waqas (an uncle of the Prophet Muhammad credited with bringing Islam to China), this is one of China’s oldest mosques, although the building has been rebuilt several times over the years. Its unusual minaret, 118 ft (36 m) high, is thought to have been used as a beacon for boats.

pois.name: Guangxiao Si
pois.text: Said to have been founded during the Western Han dynasty, Guangxiao Si (Temple of Glorious Filial Piety) is by far one of the city’s most attractive sights. Built over the palace of the last Nanyue king, Zhao Jiande, it became a temple in the 5th century and was later visited by Bodhidharma, the founder of Chan Buddhism. None of the original buildings survive, and most of the current halls date to the 19th century. The pillared main hall has several Buddha images, while the three pagodas behind it are of great antiquity. Of these, one was reportedly built over the hair of Hui Neng, the Sixth C

pois.name: Mausoleum of the Nanyue King
pois.text: In the heart of Guangzhou, next to Yuexiu Park, is the site of the 2,000-year-old tomb of Zhao Mo, the second king of Nanyue. Zhao Tuo, a Qin general from Hebei province, was sent here in 214 BCE to control southern China. After the fall of the Qin, Zhao Tuo established the Nanyue Kingdom. His grandson Zhao Mo succeeded him, reigning from 137-122 BCE. The kingdom was reclaimed by the Han kings in 111 BCE, following the hasty succession of three further Nanyue rulers. The tomb contains several magnificent burial items made of gold and precious stones, including a jade burial suit.

pois.name: Guangzhou Museum of Art
pois.text: This contemporary museum showcases works by major Chinese artists. On permanent display is an exhibition of the works of influential political cartoonist Liao Bingxiong, who was punished in 1958 for criticizing the Mao government.

pois.name: Chen Clan Ancestral Hall
pois.text: Chen Clan Ancestral Hall was built in 1890 in the gloriously colorful southern style by the Chen clan. It was to act as a temple of ancestor worship and a school. Southern-style temples are quite different from their northern counterparts. Less severely classical, their halls are generally lower and broader. Roofs and, as in the case of the first hall here, facades are often smothered in fantastic designs and figures from operas.

pois.name: OCT Loft
pois.text: It’s hard to believe this leafy neighborhood was once a district of paper mills and workers’ lodgings. Former factories have been reimagined into the epicenter of Shenzhen’s art scene - a district of art galleries, trendy bars, and upmarket restaurants. Go gallery hopping in the afternoon and stay for the evening cocktail hour.

pois.name: Dafen Oil Painting Village
pois.address: Longgang, 12 miles (20 km) NE of city
pois.text: If you’ve seen a Mona Lisa on a dentist’s wall, or The Scream in a friend’s kitchen, it was probably painted here. Now filled with galleries and cafés, Dafen makes a fun and colorful trip from downtown.

pois.name: Design Society
pois.text: Located on the western edge of Shenzhen within the international hub of Shekou, this museum celebrates the city’s design industry. Housed inside a state-of-the-art building and initially opened in partnership with London’s V&A Museum, the museum has exhibitions on Shenzhen’s manufacturing and innovation sectors, from textiles to technology.

pois.name: Shenzhen’s Theme Parks
pois.text: Shenzhen is known as the “city of theme parks” thanks to a large number of quirky attractions clustered in the Nanshan district. Window of the World comprises world monuments in miniature, while Happy Valley , just opposite, is a Disney-style fun fair. Splendid China shows off the country’s iconic architectural and geographic sites with scale models.

pois.name: Wutong Mountain
pois.address: 12 miles (20 km) NE of central Shenzhen
pois.text: A protected national park, Shenzhen’s highest peak straddles the border of Luohu and Yantian districts like a blob of green ink on a gray canvas. Locals like to hike in the hills on weekends. At the mouth of the park, Wutong Arts Village is a huddle of veggie restaurants, cafes, and artisan shops; it’s worth staying the night.

pois.name: Dapeng Peninsula
pois.address: 40 miles (70 km) E of central Shenzhen
pois.text: Set on the eastern periphery of Shenzhen, this richly forested outcrop is a fabulous place to escape the city’s modern center. On the sandy beaches of Xichong and Dongchong a nascent surf scene is evolving, while Jiaochangwei Beach is the place for windsurfers. Nearby, Dapeng Fortress is a well-preserved Ming-dynasty garrison town offering a contrasting glimpse into Shenzhen’s ancient past.

pois.name: Sanya and the South Coast
pois.text: Hainan’s main attractions are the tropical beaches near the town of Sanya, which offer good conditions for surfing. The busiest is Dadonghai, just south of town. The area’s best beach is to the east of town at Yalong Bay, with a 4-mile (7-km) stretch of pristine sand lined with upscale hotels. Tianya Haijiao, 16 miles (25 km) northwest, is known for its famous rock that appeared on the old 2-yuan note. Around 20 miles (30 km) northeast, Houhai Bay is where the surf crowd can be found.

pois.name: Haikou
pois.text: The island’s capital is a busy port and transportation hub with the ambience of a tropical Asian city. To its southeast, Wugong Ci (Five Officials Memorial Temple) was built in 1889 to honor a group of scholars who were banished here for criticizing the government. The city is also home to the excellent Hainan Museum, with informative displays on the island’s culture and history.

pois.name: Wuzhi Shan City and the Central Highlands
pois.text: The central mountainous region is worth a visit for its spectacular landscape and to explore the island’s Indigenous Li culture. Wuzhi Shan City (also known as Tongshi) is the capital of the autonomous Li and Miao governments. The Nationality Museum here offers an excellent insight into all aspects of Hainan’s history and culture. The surrounding countryside is also dotted with remnants of traditional Li houses and barns. About 30 miles (50 km) northeast of town is Wuzhi Shan, the highest peak on the island and sacred to the Li people. Farther northeast, the town of Qiongzhong is surrounded by

pois.name: The East Coast
pois.address: Wenchang: 60 miles (100 km) SE of Haikou
pois.text: The town of Wenchang is the ancestral home of the Soong sisters (see Soong Qingling’s Former Residence ) , two of whom, Qingling and Meiling, married the revolutionary leaders Sun Yat-sen and Chiang Kai-shek. Its main attractions are the beaches and coconut groves at Dongjiao Yelin and Gusong, a fishing village 25 miles (40 km) east of Wenchang. A farther 36 miles (60 km) south of Bo’ao, on the outskirts of Wanning town, Dongshan Ling has some curious rock formations. Farther south, Xinglong is well known for its coffee and for its Tropical Botanical Gardens, 2 miles (3 km) south of town. A sh

pois.name: Jianfeng Ling Nature Reserve
pois.text: Pleasantly situated in the mountains, Jianfeng Ling’s highland rain forest, with its huge trees, ferns, and vines as well as many species of birds and butterflies, offers great walks and hikes.

pois.name: Foshan
pois.text: Foshan, meaning “Buddha Mountain,” was named after three ancient bronze Buddha statues found here in the 7th century. The city has been known since the Song dynasty for its fine ceramics, particularly its distinctive figurines, characterized by a pale blue glaze. Zu Miao was founded in 1080 CE as a metallurgists’ guild temple. It is lavishly decorated with locally made ceramic figures representing scenes from traditional opera and folk stories. At the rear of the complex is a museum dedicated to Yip Man, local kung fu master and Bruce Lee’s instructor, and Wong Feihung, whose exploits have ins

pois.name: Chaozhou
pois.text: This ancient city was the seat of a highly cultured Ming-dynasty civilization. Its fortunes declined rapidly in the 17th century, when 100,000 people were massacred for opposing the conquering Qing dynasty. Later, during the 19th century, terrible famines and poverty led to mass emigration.

pois.name: Feilai and Feixia
pois.text: The busy industrial town of Qingyuan is the access point for two picturesque temples located at Feilai and Feixia on the Bei River. The temples can only be reached by boat (it’s best to charter one with a group). These depart early in the morning and return in the afternoon, passing fishers whose cormorants - trained to fish for them - sit patiently on the prows of their sampans. An hour’s journey upriver brings you to the first temple, Feilai Gusi, founded about 1,400 years ago on the steep riverbank of a gorge. Steps rise up from the water to its ornate gateway. A short walk through the fore

pois.name: Zhaoqing
pois.text: This attractive city was the home of the Italian Jesuit priest Matteo Ricci in the late 16th century, until he was expelled by a local official in 1589. Today Zhaoqing is famous for the rugged scenery at Qixing Yan (Seven Star Crag), whose misty lakeside peaks lie in the shape of the Big Bear constellation - once thought of as fallen stars. Situated a mile (1.5 km) north of the Xi River, its many shady islets, craggy hills, and illuminated caves can be explored via a vast network of bridges and causeways.

pois.name: Shaoguan
pois.text: Shaoguan town has only a handful of sights, such as the Fengcai Lou, a reconstruction of an ancient city gate, and the Dajian Chan Monastery founded in 660 CE, but there are three worthwhile places of interest near the town. The Nanhua Si (Southern China Temple), 16 miles (25 km) to the southeast, was founded in 502 CE and became renowned for its connection with Bodhidharma, the founder of Chan (Zen) Buddhism who meditated here for 36 years. One of the halls contains a statue of him, said to have been cast from his corpse; another has a statue of a monk walking on stilts made of lotus flowers.

pois.name: Cuiheng
pois.text: The village of Cuiheng, located on the outskirts of Zhongshan, is the birthplace of revolutionary leader Sun Yat-sen, also known by his Mandarin name Sun Zhongshan. He was born here in 1866. The Portuguese-style house in which he lived with his parents between 1892 and 1895 is now part of Sun Yat-sen’s Residence , a museum complex devoted to his life, along with the Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall next door, which has collected thousands of cultural artifacts and photographs. Nearby, other houses belonging to the same period have been restored and are also open to the public.

pois.name: M+
pois.text: Housed in a huge, upturned T-shaped building, M+ is Asia’s first major museum of contemporary visual culture. Its ambitious, playful exhibitions focus on 20th- and 21st-century visual art, design, film, installation art, and architecture from Hong Kong, Asia, and beyond. Past shows have featured famous names like Yayoi Kusama, Nam June Paik, and Ai Weiwei. Other highlights include the rooftop garden with sweeping harbor views and the building’s LED facade; the latter acts as a massive screen on which commissioned artworks are displayed come nightfall.

pois.name: Hong Kong Palace Museum
pois.text: This asymmetric, gold-hued building houses over 900 imperial treasures on loan from Beijing’s Forbidden City Palace Museum, many never before seen outside the capital. Stylish galleries showcase China’s rich history, arts and culture, with items on display including Qing court robes and Song-dynasty ceramics, as well as rare calligraphy, bronzeware, and religious sculpture. Exhibits rotate regularly, and some galleries require timed tickets (see website for details).

pois.name: West Kowloon Art Park
pois.text: A breezy expanse of green space between the big venues, this harbor-side park is perfect for a stroll or a picnic on the Great Lawn. There are kiosks for coffee and snacks, too. Things get more lively at weekends, when food trucks roll in and pop-up events, mini festivals, and performances add energy to the park.

pois.name: Xiqu Centre
pois.text: Covered by woven metal panels designed to look like silk curtains, the Xiqu Centre is the cutting-edge home for the long-standing art form of Cantonese opera. Inside, there’s a soaring atrium, as well as two theaters: the Grand Theatre, which stages full-length performances (often with English subtitles), and the smaller Tea House Theatre, offering narrated 90-minute shows with tea and dim sum, perfect for those enjoying Cantonese opera for the first time. Book tickets for performances via the WestK website or at the Xiqu box office.

pois.name: West Kowloon Waterfront Promenade
pois.text: Skirting the edge of Victoria Harbour, this waterfront promenade has panoramic views west to forested Lantau and south to the illuminated skyline of Central. It’s a popular spot with joggers, walkers, cyclists, and families, with plenty of seating dotted about, as well as art installations and drinks vendors.

pois.name: Freespace
pois.text: This venue showcases the performing arts, including contemporary theater, music, and dance. The main hall is used for bold, often experimental shows, while the open-air stage outside hosts regular festivals and free gigs. Don’t miss the vibrant mural by Hong Kong artist Calvin Ho found next to the venue.

pois.name: Fortaleza do Monte
pois.text: Built between 1617 and 1626, this fortress overlooked the original Portuguese settlement at Macau. Its thick ramparts, surmounted by ancient cannons, still occupy a commanding position and appear as invincible as they did back in 1622, when the invading Dutch forces were defeated. Dug into the hill beneath the fort is the informative Macau Museum . Its stairs and escalators provide an air-conditioned route to the hilltop fortress, passing through re-creations of Portuguese and Chinese life. Beginning with the arrival of Portuguese traders and Jesuit missionaries, the exhibitions on the first f

pois.name: Old Protestant Cemetery
pois.text: This cemetery was founded in 1821 by the British East India Company. Prior to this, Protestants in Macau had to secretly bury their dead outside the city walls at night, due to restrictions on burials both inside the Roman Catholic Portuguese colony and in the Chinese territory beyond.

pois.name: Ruinas de São Paulo
pois.text: All that is left of this once grand cathedral, built by the Jesuits and perched precariously atop a steep flight of steps, is its magnificent, crumbling facade. Its most outstanding features are the facade’s ornate figures, which include a “sermon in stone” that records some of the main events from the Christian scriptures, interwoven with East Asian motifs such as chrysanthemums, lotus flowers, and several mythic creatures.

pois.name: The Venetian
pois.text: Inspired by The Venetian in Las Vegas, Macau’s most spectacular hotel-casino re-creates a miniature Venice, which is complete with campanile, Rialto Bridge, and gondolas with singing gondoliers. The mega-resort consists of suites only and offers themed shopping as well as a theater seating up to 1,800 people. There is the usual array of slot machines, blackjack, baccarat, roulette, and keno (similar to bingo), as well as some Chinese games, including the dice game dai siu and the mahjong-style pai gow . Gambling is Macau’s lifeblood, contributing more than half the government’s revenue. In fac

pois.name: Guia Fort and Lighthouse
pois.text: The Guia Fort was built between 1622 and 1638 and offers great views over the town. Initially it served as a fort to defend the border with China, but in 1865 a lighthouse was added. A pleasant way to get here is to take the cable car to the hilltop. A small chapel stands next door and there are several gentle walking trails around the hill.

pois.name: Praia Grande
pois.text: Perhaps the best way to get a flavor of Macau’s historic architecture is to take a stroll along the Avenida de Praia Grande. Although land reclamation has encroached on the waterfront and robbed the Praia Grande of some of its elegance, it is still a charming place, with many grand houses dating to the 1800s and early 1900s.

pois.name: Largo do Senado
pois.text: The symbolic heart of Macau, the Largo do Senado or Senate Square has a number of stately colonial buildings set around it. Notable buildings include the Leal Senado, or Loyal Senate, which now houses Macau’s Municipal Affairs Bureau; the General Post Office; and the Santa Casa de Misericordia, an old refuge for orphans and the poor and destitute. There are also numerous shops, cafés, and restaurants in the area. The striking, wavy black-and-white tile patterns snaking across the square make it a great place to take photographs by day or night.

pois.name: Rua da Felicidade
pois.text: A variety of sweet scents waft from the Rua da Felicidade, or “Street of Happiness,” where tasty and colorful Macanese biscuits and cakes are baked and sold. The area was once packed with brothels, hence its somewhat ironically bestowed name. Today, it is a charming, cobbled street lined with small eateries, teahouses, and souvenir shops.

pois.name: Museu de Art de Macau
pois.text: With individual galleries spread across five floors of a starkly Modernist building, this well-run museum features works that run the gamut from colonial-era oil paintings to contemporary Chinese photography. There is also an excellent collection of antique ceramics and other archaeological finds, plus classical Chinese calligraphy. The museum has an ever-changing roster of temporary exhibitions, often featuring work by well-known contemporary international and Chinese artists.

pois.name: Macau Tower
pois.text: The Macau Tower, the peninsula’s most visible attraction, is 1,107 ft (338 m) high. The tower provides a great view; in fact, visitors can see Hong Kong’s surrounding islands on a clear day. However, it is not the ideal place for those who don’t like heights. Glass-sided elevators rocket visitors skyward, and the restaurants and viewing galleries at the top are also partially glass-bottomed. The truly adventurous can even don overalls and a harness and explore parts of the tower’s exterior with the adventure sports company A. J. Hackett, which runs a number of activities, including bungee jump

pois.name: The Barra
pois.text: Located just south of Largo do Senado, Rua Central and Rua P. Antonio cut through the Barra district, which is where Macau’s first European residents settled. Today, the Barra is a popular spot buzzing with excellent restaurants.

pois.name: Maritime Museum
pois.text: Small-scale but interesting exhibits make this museum worth a visit for insights into the maritime past upon which Macau’s wealth was built. Displays include models of Chinese junks, Portuguese ships and fishing boats, a mock Hakka village, a dragon boat, and a detailed scale model of old Macau. A highlight is the Little A-Ma Theatre, which tells the legend of a local goddess. There is also a nice bar located on the esplanade outside, which is open during museum hours.

pois.name: Central
pois.text: The sleek, corporate cathedrals of banks and businesses tower over the ever-teeming streets of Hong Kong’s financial epicenter. There are relatively few cultural sights in Central, as many colonial buildings have long since disappeared, making way for high-rise development. The desire for real estate has always been strong, and land reclamation started almost as soon as the British took over in 1841. This continuous creation of new land has made Hong Kong Island and Kowloon creep ever closer. Central is easily explored on foot, giving you a close-up look at some of the most interesting buildin

pois.name: Wan Chai
pois.text: Immortalized in Richard Mason’s 1957 novel The World of Suzy Wong , Wan Chai’s colorful red light district has now largely given way to fancy bars, restaurants, and hotels. The Wan Chai Metro Rail Transit (MTR) station is a good starting point for a walking tour. A trip down Lockhart Road, just around the corner, reveals the area’s few remaining ties with its past in the form of a handful of hostess bars.

pois.name: Causeway Bay
pois.text: A neon crush of malls, giant department stores, and the ever-present crowds of shoppers will likely be your first impression of Causeway Bay upon emerging from the MTR. East of the station is Victoria Park, Hong Kong’s largest park and a serene place to swim, play tennis, or practice your Tai Chi. Close to the Typhoon Shelter is the Noonday Gun, a blue 3-lb (1.5-kg) artillery gun that has been fired daily since the 1840s. The enclosure housing the gun opens for 30 minutes after noon, where a small plaque explains the origins of the tradition, celebrated in Noel Coward’s 1931 song “Mad Dogs and

pois.name: Man Mo Temple
pois.text: Atmospheric Man Mo Temple stands at the corner of Ladder Street. Inside its red-and-gold interior, smoke curls from giant incense spirals hanging from the ceiling, and flames in large brass urns devour paper offerings to the dead, such as the ubiquitous Hell banknotes. Built in 1847, the temple was dedicated to two deities, Man and Mo (gods of literature and war), both based on real people - the 3rd-century administrator Cheung Ah Tse and the 3rd-century soldier Kwan Yu - who were deified by the emperors. Their statues can be seen at the back of the main chamber. Set in the historic heart of t

pois.name: Hong Kong Zoological and Botanical Gardens
pois.text: Opposite Hong Kong Park, just across Cotton Tree Drive, lie the expansive Zoological and Botanical Gardens, established in 1864. The gardens house dozens of animals such as lemurs, meerkats, sloths and monkeys, while its aviaries are filled with colorful birds from all over the world, including American flamingos and Bali mynahs. There are also hundreds of plants, including some ancient trees, which provide welcome shade in this quiet oasis. You’ll even find striking sculptures and fountains dotted around the gardens, as well as a children’s play area.

pois.name: Tai Kwun
pois.text: An early 20th-century police compound, Tai Kwun underwent the biggest restoration program in Hong Kong history. It is now a mixed-use arts and culture center heritage museum, as well as a drinking and dining destination. It is home to the famed art gallery, J.C. Contemporary, as well as a list of restaurants and bars.

pois.name: Lan Kwai Fong
pois.text: Although its popularity has diminished since the COVID-19 pandemic and the protests, Lan Kwai Fong (“Orchid Square”) is still one of Hong Kong’s party corners, often filled with locals, tourists, and visitors across from the mainland. It’s a great place to start out in the city if you’re looking for a livelier night out, with a seemingly endless array of restaurants, bars, and nightclubs offering something for everyone. Dress formally and enjoy fine dining and wine pairings, or come as you are and find a bar to prop up. The main stretch is on D’Aguilar Street, which mostly comes alive on weeke

pois.name: Star Ferry
pois.address: Terminals: Central, Wan Chai, and Kowloon
pois.text: Touted as Hong Kong Island’s most dependable sight, the Star Ferry service was started in 1898 by Indian Parsi businessman Dorabjee Nowrojee Mithaiwala. Today, few activities in Hong Kong can compete with the excitement and romance of riding one of these iconic double-decker ferries as they chug ponderously between Kowloon and Hong Kong Island. They are by far the best and cheapest way to view the city skyline by day or night, with an air-conditioned cabin and open-air deck to enjoy. Some 70,000 passengers travel on Star Ferry’s small fleet every day.

pois.name: Hong Kong Museum of Art
pois.text: Reopened in late 2019 after a lavish and lengthy renovation, the Hong Kong Museum of Art’s new facilities have doubled the number of galleries, including a new one on the roof, and increased the exhibition space to house monumental contemporary art. Two innovative restaurants have also been added: modern gourmet Australian restaurant Hue, and alfresco restaurant Ink, specializing in light snacks and seafood.

pois.name: Hong Kong Science Museum
pois.address: Science Museum Road, Tsim Sha Tsui
pois.text: An excellent destination for children, the Science Museum is packed with fun interactive displays on its four floors that detail basic scientific principles, including electricity and gravity, and a fun “World of Mirrors” on the first floor. As well as informative exhibits on the natural and life sciences, you’ll find many displays on technology, which detail the workings of various types of machinery ranging from the combustion engine to computer chips, as well as robotics and virtual reality. The centerpiece of the museum is the giant “Energy Machine,” which runs through four stories of the

pois.name: Hong Kong Museum of History
pois.hours: 10am-6pm Mon, Wed-Fri; 10am-7pm Sat, Sun, & public hols
pois.address: 100 Chatham Road S, Tsim Sha Tsui E
pois.text: The Museum of History was once home to the excellent Hong Kong Story, an exhibition that traced the area’s rich history, from its geological origins to its present day. However, pressure from the mainland government has resulted in the exhibit’s temporary closure and the opening of a new - and propaganda-heavy - permanent gallery on national security. There is also a display of Bronze Age daggers, pottery, and arrowheads from Lamma and Lantau islands.

pois.name: Tsim Sha Tsui Waterfront
pois.text: The Tsim Sha Tsui promenade features some of the ritziest arcades, museums, and hotels in the city, as well as the famous Star Ferry pier. East of the pier is the iconic Hong Kong Cultural Centre, which houses a concert hall and theater. Next to the Centre is the Hong Kong Space Museum , with fun, interactive exhibits and a “space theater.” Other attractions include the Avenue of Stars, honoring the city’s film greats, and an elevated walkway.

pois.name: Happy Valley Racecourse
pois.text: The racecourse at Happy Valley crackles with beer-fueled energy during the Wednesday race nights, as tens of thousands of eager revellers shout their way through the evening. Horse-racing is a passion in Hong Kong; it’s one of the few legal gambling opportunities available to locals. The industry is highly regulated, with only the Hong Kong Jockey Club allowed to run the betting.

pois.name: Temple Street and Jade Markets
pois.text: Haggling is an essential skill at the Temple Street night market, which snakes north from Ning Po Street to Man Ming Lane and only livens up after 8pm. Although cheaper bargains are available elsewhere, the atmosphere and range of items, including fake designer labels, shoes, and Mao memorabilia, are unbeatable. Adding to the experience are fortune-tellers, street performers, and various food vendors.

pois.name: Wong Tai Sin Temple
pois.text: The temple at Wong Tai Sin is one of Hong Kong’s largest, busiest, and most fascinating places of worship. The complex contains altars and shrines to Buddhist, Confucian, and Daoist deities, though it is primarily dedicated to the Daoist deity Wong Tai Sin, a 4th-century shepherd and later monk, reputed to have performed healing miracles. Accordingly, the temple is frequently visited by people hoping to cure or avoid illness. Beside the main temple you’ll find dozens of fortune-tellers, some of whom can reveal your fortune in English (albeit for a fee), mostly through palm and face reading.

pois.name: Flower Market
pois.address: Flower Market Road, Mong Kok, Kowloon
pois.text: The Flower Market is a less frenetic and more convenient setting than Temple Street, and is well worth a casual browse. Colorful blooms and clever bamboo creations line Flower Market Road, just north of Prince Edward Road West. A huge array of cut flowers, potted plants, seeds, and bulbs are sold throughout the year.

pois.name: 10,000 Buddhas Monastery
pois.address: 221 Pai Tau Village, Sha Tin, New Territories
pois.text: Ruby-lipped, life-size golden arhats (people who have attained nirvana) line the steep path up to the modern 10,000 Buddhas Monastery, a 15-minute walk from the northern exit of the Sha Tin MTR station. Cross the road and follow the clear signposts to the temple, which sits at the top of the wooded hill. The main temple houses hundreds of miniature golden Buddhas that line shelves reaching up to the ceiling.

pois.name: Heritage Museum
pois.address: 1 Man Lam Road, Sha Tin, New Territories
pois.text: This excellent modern museum tells the story of Hong Kong’s 6,000-year-old human history. The largest of the city’s many museums, it has five permanent exhibitions and plenty of space for temporary shows.

pois.name: Sai Kung Town and Peninsula Beaches
pois.metro: Choi Hung, then taxi or minibus 1A or 1S to Sai Kung Town
pois.text: It might be a hard thing to imagine, but just 10 miles (16 km) from Kowloon’s busy streets are empty beaches, clear surf, and seclusion on the shores of the rugged Sai Kung Peninsula. Sai Kung is also home to the stunning Hong Kong Global Geopark, which was formed by ancient volcanic eruptions. It is known for its polygonal rock columns and hidden sea caves.

pois.name: Kadoorie Farm and Botanic Garden
pois.text: This working organic farm and wildlife refuge is nestled in the wooded foothills of Hong Kong’s tallest mountain, Tai Mo Shan. It is a great place to escape downtown, with an easy hike to the top. There are terraced vegetable plots and fruit groves, an animal enclosure with wildcats, deer, and birds of prey, and a walking trail. You will need a good half-day to see everything on offer.

pois.name: Ocean Park
pois.text: Ever since the arrival of Hong Kong Disneyland , Ocean Park, Hong Kong’s first amusement park, has considerably upped its game. It now gives Disney a run for its money, attracting huge crowds every day.

pois.name: Deep Water and Repulse Bays
pois.text: Several beaches line these two scenic bays located along the road from Aberdeen to Stanley. Deep Water Bay is an attractive spot favored by the wealthy, with luxurious houses and a pristine stretch of beach lined by cypress-like trees, redolent of the French Riviera.

pois.name: Mai Po Marshes
pois.metro: Sheung Shui, then 76K bus or taxi
pois.text: Wedged between Hong Kong and the vast urban sprawl of Shenzhen, this globally important wetland managed by the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) is home to a huge range of wildlife species. Pollution has taken its toll elsewhere along the Pearl River delta, making this huge park the last refuge for many species. Thousands of migratory birds flock here to feed on crustaceans and small fish. Apart from the ubiquitous herons and egrets, otters and the endangered black-faced spoonbill - of which only some 2,000 are left in the world - can be seen here. There are many bird hides dotted about for keen bird-

pois.name: Aberdeen
pois.text: Once a quiet fishing village, Aberdeen is today the largest separate town on Hong Kong Island. Named in 1845 after the British Colonial Secretary, the Earl of Aberdeen, the harbor housed the city’s first dockyard, which was built in the 1860s.

pois.name: Stanley
pois.text: This pre-colonial fishing village today resembles a British seaside town, complete with English-style pubs. The extensive sprawl of market stalls selling clothes, beachwear, silk, jade, trinkets, and furniture draws weekend crowds. The area also has a good selection of Thai, Italian, Spanish, Vietnamese, and Chinese restaurants.

pois.name: Lamma Island
pois.text: Great seafood and pubs, a relaxed atmosphere, pleasant hilltop walks, and the absence of cars make leafy Lamma the perfect escape from the city bustle. Its two main villages, Yung Shue Wan on the west coast and restaurant-packed Sok Kwu Wan on the east coast, are a half-hour ferry ride from Central. A steep climb leads to the hills above Yung Shue Wan, where you can enjoy wonderful views of the sea and Hong Kong Island. You can hike between the two villages, but plan your walk around the infrequent ferries. The harbor at Sok Kwu Wan is home to Lamma Fisherfolk’s Village, a floating exhibition

pois.name: Cheung Chau Island
pois.text: This charming island, a mere 45 minutes by ferry from Hong Kong Island, has plenty to offer, including beautiful beaches, traditional shops and shrines, and a tantalizing array of seafood restaurants at the harbor’s edge on Pak She Praya Road. Squid with shrimp paste is a local specialty. The southern coast offers the best walks, with great sea views and woodland paths threaded through striking rock formations.

pois.name: Lantau Island
pois.metro: Tung Chung, then taxi or cable car
pois.text: Twice the size of Hong Kong Island, Lantau was ceded to the British in 1898 along with the other islands and the New Territories. Despite the addition of a bridge and the huge airport at Chek Lap Kok, large tracts of the island remain virtually uninhabited.
